prize_parts.citation: for empirical evidence on how exposure to import competition reshapes local labour markets, employment and wages, and on how those markets adjust

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is still B036 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The laureate set is unchanged from round 1. The wording has changed. I have dropped 'technological change' from the citation and anchored it on exposure to import competition and local-labour-market adjustment. In round 1 I argued that a narrow citation should not be read as a verdict on the technology strand. Keeping 'technological change' in the citation text contradicted that, and it implied credit for the task framework that this trio cannot carry cleanly. Autor and Dorn have separate work on automation and polarisation, but Hanson is not part of that strand, and Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane have claims outside the credited set. The case rests on three things. First, the question is first-order: who bears the adjustment costs of trade, and how long does the burden last? Second, the designs are transparent, and that is why they could be criticised, replicated and extended over a decade. Third, attribution to the three jointly authored papers is tighter than for any other entry that I rank highly. I take the central, robust finding to be that import exposure lowered employment and wages in exposed local markets and that adjustment was slow. The long-run magnitude is a separate matter and remains debated. The citation should state the first and say nothing about the second. After reading the round-1 exchange, my view of merit has not changed. My view of the credit has become firmer. The seven-member convergence on the same trio came largely from members revising their ballots, and I do not treat it as scientific evidence. I have tested the attribution against Katz, against Strömberg's Autor-Katz pairing, and against Friberg's maturity objection, and it still holds.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is identification and interpretation. The shift-share exposure measures and instruments are contested. The long-run size and persistence of the effects are not settled. The trade-versus-automation split is also debated. The 2021 speech I gave stressed that natural-experiment evidence is harder to interpret than a controlled trial, and the same caution applies to a prize on this work. The ballot entry also bundles two strands, and my narrower citation leaves the task and skill-premium lineage uncredited. That means Katz, and parts of the lineage involving Acemoglu (2024), Levy and Murnane, go unrecognised. Thematic overlap with the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes is real. I would want the Committee to say openly that this is a prize about trade exposure and local labour markets and not a ruling on the origin of the task framework. I also cannot rule out that B034 has a cleaner credit structure once the priority questions are better understood. I hold this as a serious doubt about my own ordering.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson now prefers Autor, Dorn and Hanson after moving from Katz to Dorn. She wants a citation about technology and trade exposure, and says the Committee should state that the prize rests on the design and the robust finding of persistent adjustment costs, not on a particular elasticity. She also says Autor links the two strands.
responses.response: I agree that the prize should rest on the design and the finding, and not on an elasticity. I differ on the technology half of the wording. Autor does span both strands, but the citation names three people, and only two of them have work on technology and tasks. A citation that includes 'technological change and wage inequality' asks the credited trio to carry credit for the task framework, and that framework's originators sit outside the credited set. This is why I changed my wording and dropped 'technological change'. I accept that this makes the prize narrower than the ballot title. I would sooner have a narrow prize with defensible credit than a broad citation that the Committee would have to defend against Katz, Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane. I also note that you moved off Katz partly because of overlap with the 2023 prize. That argument applies to the technology wording of the citation, not only to the name list.

responses.point: Andersson moved from an Autor-Hanson-Katz trio to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. He argues that persistence determines whether the contribution is a lasting discovery or a contested estimate, and says the citation should be worded around exposure and adjustment and should avoid claiming a precise effect size. He keeps B018 as an alternative because of the attribution cap.
responses.response: I agree with that framing of the citation and have adopted it in my wording. I would add one criterion. A claim about persistence should be treated as a claim about adjustment, such as mobility, transfers and employment rates. It should not be treated as a claim about a stable aggregate number. The finding that adjustment was slow and concentrated is the part that has survived re-examination in your own and others' accounts. On B018, we reach the same place by the same route. The scientific importance is very high, and the obstacle is the three-name cap. That obstacle is a defect in the choice, not in the field, and I would not want it to count against B036 by default.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B036 seventh and doubts that the maturity bar is met because of ongoing debate on identification, persistence and magnitude. He says he would not oppose it. His own preference is the demand-estimation entry (B020), which he defends on maturity and reach, and he accepts that structural estimates are sensitive to instruments and functional form.
responses.response: I take the maturity objection seriously, and the chair has asked what would change my mind. I would revise my view if re-examination of the shift-share designs showed that the employment and wage effects in exposed markets were not robust to corrected inference or to alternative exposure measures. A finding that the persistence was driven mainly by something other than import exposure would have the same effect. I have not independently checked those re-examinations, and I rely on what colleagues' files report: the central finding survived in qualified form and the magnitudes were refined. I also note that your own B020 case concedes that structural estimates are sensitive to specification. Sensitivity of magnitudes does not by itself defeat a discovery, either in your candidate or in mine. Where we really differ is on whether the finding is mature enough. I put the line at whether the qualitative result survives scrutiny. I think it has.

responses.point: Enflo prefers B034 with Helpman and Melitz. She argues it is less exposed than B036 because it has no comparable dispute about magnitudes and no adjacent recent prize. She reads the China-shock record as more mixed than 'held up', and separates Krugman's 2008 contribution from selection and reallocation across firms.
responses.response: Your separation of the 2008 prize from selection and reallocation is persuasive, and it has weakened one of my reservations about B034. I am less convinced by the claim that B034 has no magnitude dispute. Your own and Strömberg's files record that the size of welfare gains depends on model structure and parametrisation, and that priority questions with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are unresolved. That is a different kind of uncertainty from the one in B036, but it is not smaller. On B036, I accept that the record is mixed on size and on persistence. I would describe it as robust on sign and on local concentration, which is why I want a citation that makes no claim about size. I keep B034 as my first alternative. If the Committee judged the priority question answerable, I would find it a close call between the two on scientific grounds.

responses.point: Krusell keeps B018 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford as his preferred part and lists B036 as his first alternative. He says my attribution argument moved him on the trio, and he asks whether Taylor or Galí should be the third name. He concedes that credit is spread over at least eight contributors.
responses.response: I appreciate the move on the trio, but I do not want it counted as support for B036 over B018, and I do not read it that way. On your question: I proposed Woodford, Taylor and Calvo in round 1, and I still think that is the most defensible trio, because Taylor's rule links the theory to how policy is conducted. I cannot say it is a founding contribution rather than a cut. Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets did work that made the framework operational, and any trio omits them. That is the main reason B018 is an alternative for me and not my preferred part. The post-2008 and 2021-23 experience is, in my view, a test of the framework and not a defeat of it, so I agree with you that it does not settle the question. It does reinforce the attribution problem.

uncertainties: Whether the exposure-based findings on employment, wages and adjustment are robust to corrected inference for shift-share designs and to alternative exposure measures. I have not independently verified this and rely on what colleagues' files report.

Whether the Committee accepts a citation limited to import competition and local-labour-market adjustment, or insists on a broader technology-and-labour citation that brings in Katz and the task lineage with its overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes.
Whether the attribution cost of leaving out Katz and the task framework originators (including Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane) is acceptable. I think it is, but it is a real cost.
Whether the priority questions around B034 (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum, Yeaple) can be answered, which would affect how I rank it against B036.
Whether the seven-member convergence on B036 reflects independent assessment or the order of the exchange. I treat it as untested information, not as merit evidence.
statement.conflict_note: I have no co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Dorn, Hanson or Katz in my supplied profile, nor to Helpman, Melitz, Calvo, Taylor or Woodford. I disclose field proximity: my research is in empirical labour economics and policy evaluation using quasi-experimental designs, which may make me more receptive to design-based work like B036. As chair I gave the 2021 presentation speech on the prize for natural-experiment methods, and the 2021 Scientific Background cites my 2013 class-size paper with Öckert and Oosterbeek. That is a methodological affinity, not a tie to the candidates. My long-standing co-authors include Holmlund, Edin, Åslund, Öckert, Johansson, Nybom, Oosterbeek and van Ours, none of whom appear on these ballot items. Holmlund is also listed as a frequent co-author of Hjalmarsson, which is a collegial tie and not a tie to any candidate. I overlapped at Stockholm University with the IIES macro group (Hassler, Krusell) in 2010-17, which was an institutional overlap and not co-authorship. I do not adjudicate any of these.
